title: Evidence before you ship
glance: A few good-looking examples, or a test that changed two things at once, is not evidence: run the eval set first, change one thing at a time, then pick the live test that fits the question.
story: When someone rewrites a prompt and tries it on ten conversations, the answers often look better. That feeling is an anecdote: ten hand-picked cases cannot show whether the change broke something on the other hundreds of kinds of question. The cheap, safe first step is the offline eval: run the old and new versions on the same full test set and compare the scores.

Once the offline eval passes, the next step depends on the question being asked. If the question is about real user behaviour (do more customers finish, do fewer call back), you need an A/B test: a random share of live traffic gets the new version, the rest keep the old one, over the same period. If traffic is too low for an A/B test to reach a clear answer, roll out in stages with close monitoring and a rollback. If showing users an unapproved answer is not allowed, run it in shadow: live inputs, outputs compared but never shown.

Two rules sit under all of this. Change one thing at a time, or nobody can say which change caused the result. And the same discipline applies to new model versions: a newer model is adopted through the eval suite and a staged rollout, not because it is newer.
situation: A letting agency's tenant assistant answers questions about leases and repairs, about 3,000 conversations a day. An engineer has rewritten the system prompt, and on ten conversations she tried, the answers read better. The team keeps an offline eval set of 400 past questions with expected answers. What should the team do next with the new prompt?

options.t: Run the new and current prompts on the full 400-question eval set and compare them.
A/B test the new prompt against the current one on a random half of live traffic.
Run the new prompt in shadow on live messages, comparing outputs without showing tenants.
Release the new prompt to a tenth of tenants, widening only if monitored metrics hold.

worlds.name: As written
worlds.fact: Only the ten conversations the engineer picked have been tried. Nothing else has been run.
worlds.why: Ten examples are an anecdote. The offline eval is cheap, covers 400 cases with expected answers, and catches regressions before any tenant sees the new prompt.

losers.B: An A/B test would expose half of all tenants to a prompt that may have broken cases the ten examples never touched. It comes after the offline eval, not instead of it.
losers.C: Shadow outputs have no expected answers, so someone must grade them by hand. The eval set already has expected answers, so it is the cheaper first check.
losers.D: A staged release limits the damage, but it still puts an unchecked prompt in front of real tenants. Staging follows the eval; it does not replace it.

worlds.name: Eval passed; a business question
worlds.fact: The new prompt passed the full eval set with slightly better scores. The owner now asks whether it raises the share of repair requests settled without a call-back from the tenant.
worlds.why: Call-backs are tenant behaviour, which only real tenants can show. A random split over the same period, at 3,000 conversations a day, gives a clear answer quickly.

losers.A: Already done. The eval set measures answer quality, not whether tenants call back.
losers.C: Shadow answers never reach tenants, so they cannot change whether tenants call back. It measures outputs, not behaviour.
losers.D: A staged release has no control group running at the same time, so a change in call-backs could come from the season or a new repair backlog rather than the prompt.

worlds.name: Eval passed; low traffic
worlds.fact: The new prompt passed the full eval set, but the assistant serves a small agency and handles about 30 conversations a day. An A/B test would need many months to give a clear result.
worlds.why: With offline evidence in hand and too little traffic for an A/B test, a staged release with close monitoring and a ready rollback is the practical way to gather live evidence safely.

losers.A: Already done and passed. Running it again adds nothing new.
losers.B: At 30 conversations a day the test would run for months before the difference was clear, which delays a change the eval already supports.
losers.C: Shadow adds hand-grading work on live messages but still says nothing about how tenants respond. Nothing in this world forbids showing tenants the new prompt.

signals: “changed the prompt and the model in the same release”
“passed the offline eval; does it raise…?”
“traffic is too low for a clear result”
“policy forbids showing users an unapproved version”
remember: Evidence comes in order: the offline eval first, then the live test that fits the question (A/B for behaviour, shadow when exposure is forbidden, staged rollout when traffic is low). Change one thing at a time.

practice.stem: A legal publisher's research assistant lost five points on its eval suite after one release that changed both the retrieval chunk size and the answer prompt. Users have not noticed yet. The team wants to keep whichever change helped and drop the one that hurt. What should the team do?
options: Revert the whole release, then test each change on its own against the eval suite.
Keep the release live and add eval cases until the cause of the drop becomes clear.
Revert only the prompt change, as prompt edits are the usual cause of quality drops.
A/B test the full release against the previous version on a share of live traffic.
practice.why: The deciding fact: two things changed at once, and the team wants to know which one hurt. Reverting stops the regression, and testing each change alone shows which to keep.
traps: Works, but it leaves a known drop live, and more cases still cannot separate two changes made together.
Works if the prompt was the cause, but that is a guess; the chunk size may be what hurt.
Works for measuring user impact, but it still tests both changes together and exposes users to the drop.

practice.stem: A bank's card-support assistant is moving to a newer model version, which scored better on the full eval suite. The suite was built two years ago from English conversations. Since then, a third of conversations arrive in Spanish, and no eval case is in Spanish. What should the team do before moving traffic?
options: Begin a staged rollout now, since the suite already shows the new version is better.
Run an A/B test on live traffic to see how Spanish-speaking customers respond.
Add Spanish cases taken from real conversations to the suite, then rerun both versions.
Ask a few Spanish-speaking staff to try the new version and report their impressions.
practice.why: The deciding fact: a third of real traffic is in a language the suite never tests, so the pass says nothing about it. Adding real Spanish cases makes the evidence cover current usage.
traps: Works when the suite covers today's usage; here a third of traffic is untested.
Works for user behaviour once offline checks pass, but here it exposes Spanish speakers to an unchecked version.
Works as a quick sense check, but a few impressions are anecdotes, not evidence.

practice.stem: A logistics firm is moving its tracking assistant to a newer model version. The new version needs tool definitions in a new format, and the old format does not work with it. The team plans one release with both changes. A reviewer insists they must test one change at a time. What is the best approach?
options: Test the new tool format alone on the current model, then add the model upgrade.
Run the eval suite on the combined release against the current version, then stage it.
Ship both changes together, since the provider recommends the newer model version.
Test the model upgrade first on its own, then move to the new format in a later release.
practice.why: The deciding fact: the two changes cannot work apart, so they are one change. Test the pair as a unit on the eval suite, then roll out in stages.
traps: Works when each change stands alone; here the format exists only to serve the new model.
Works, but a provider's recommendation is not evidence for your task; the eval must run first.
Works for independent changes, but the new model cannot run with the old format, so this test is impossible.
